periods.analysis: Harborview closed 2024-Q3 in a controlled position: Procurement Cycle Time was 30 days, exactly at the <=30-day target, and Invoices Paid Within 30 Days was 98.4%, comfortably above the >=95% target. This is a green result, but I would call the cycle-time margin thin rather than generous. The Purchasing desk cleared several late-summer public works and fleet requisitions through the standard Munis workflow, and the AP team’s Tuesday/Thursday check-run discipline kept vendor payments current. From a controls standpoint, the quarter shows that speed did not require bypassing approval gates.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the twice-weekly AP check-run schedule and keep the 30-day procurement aging report on the Finance & Administration dashboard. For 2024-Q4, add a weekly exception review for requisitions sitting more than 12 business days in department approval, with named follow-up by buyer. Keep using standard competitive templates for fleet, facilities, and parks purchases so the city preserves both cycle time and audit defensibility.

periods.analysis: In 2024-Q4, Procurement Cycle Time improved from 30 days to 28 days, a 2-day quarter-over-quarter reduction while remaining green against the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days declined from 98.4% to 97.5%, down 0.9 percentage points, but still well above the >=95% control threshold. The improvement in procurement timing appears tied to early bundling of winter maintenance, janitorial, and IT support renewals under the Q4 Renewal Calendar. The payment dip was modest and traceable to year-end receiving delays, not a systemic AP backlog.
periods.recommendations: Continue the Q4 Renewal Calendar approach and extend it to recurring service contracts expiring in March and April. Require departments to receipt goods in Munis within two business days during year-end close to protect the payment metric. Finance should also sample ten delayed invoices from Q4 and document whether the delay was vendor, department receiving, or AP processing.

periods.analysis: The 2025-Q1 results strengthened materially: Procurement Cycle Time moved from 28 days to 23 days, a 5-day quarter-over-quarter improvement and well below the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days moved from 97.5% to 96.3%, down 1.2 percentage points, but remained green above the >=95% target. The faster procurement result reflects effective use of the Buyer Intake Queue and pre-approved specifications for police body-worn camera accessories, pump-station electrical parts, and library technology refresh items. I am comfortable with the result, provided we keep watching the gradual payment-rate erosion across two quarters.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the Buyer Intake Queue as the standard front door for purchases over the department quote threshold. Assign AP to review the 2025-Q1 invoices paid after 30 days and separate preventable coding delays from legitimate vendor disputes. To sustain the green position, publish a short department checklist for receiving, account coding, and contract reference numbers before the April close.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q2, Procurement Cycle Time increased from 23 days to 26 days, a 3-day quarter-over-quarter increase, but stayed green against the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days improved from 96.3% to 96.7%, up 0.4 percentage points and still above the >=95% target. The cycle-time increase is not unexpected given spring construction solicitations, including pavement preservation packages, marina restroom repairs, and Parks irrigation controls. The important control point is that the added days came from advertised bid periods and legal review, not stalled approvals.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the spring construction solicitation calendar, but add a procurement milestone tracker for any bid with a planned award date before Council recess. Continue AP’s coding-delay review and send department-specific exception lists every Friday until the payment rate is consistently above 97%. For green sustainment, pre-load standard insurance, bond, and prevailing-wage clauses into the bid library before the next paving cycle.

periods.analysis: The 2025-Q3 result remains green, though it is closer to the procurement limit: Procurement Cycle Time rose from 26 days to 29 days, a 3-day quarter-over-quarter increase versus the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days improved from 96.7% to 97.4%, up 0.7 percentage points and safely above the >=95% target. The longer procurement cycle reflects summer workload and several higher-risk solicitations, including coastal path lighting, fire station HVAC controls, and on-call engineering panels. Payment performance improved because departments responded better to AP exception lists and because receiving was handled earlier in the workflow.
periods.recommendations: Treat the 29-day procurement cycle time as a watch item even though the overall status is green. For 2025-Q4, have Purchasing triage all open solicitations each Monday into standard, complex, and Council-sensitive lanes, with escalation after day 20. Preserve the AP gains by continuing Friday exception lists and adding automatic reminders to project managers with open purchase orders older than 21 days.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q4, Procurement Cycle Time improved from 29 days to 26 days, a 3-day quarter-over-quarter reduction and a return to more comfortable room under the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days decreased from 97.4% to 95.8%, down 1.6 percentage points, but remained green above the >=95% target. The procurement improvement suggests the solicitation triage lanes worked, especially for the copier fleet replacement, fuel card renewal, and harbor security camera maintenance contract. The payment decline is acceptable but close enough to the control floor that I would not treat it as noise; year-end receiving and grant-coding reviews created friction.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Monday solicitation triage process and make it permanent for complex purchases and Council-sensitive awards. For payments, require year-end receiving certification from departments with more than 15 open purchase orders, beginning with Public Works, Parks, and IT. AP should run a December closeout huddle with Grants and Budget staff so grant-coded invoices do not sit while funding strings are corrected.

periods.analysis: The 2026-Q1 performance improved on both controls: Procurement Cycle Time moved from 26 days to 24 days, a 2-day quarter-over-quarter reduction, and Invoices Paid Within 30 Days moved from 95.8% to 96.6%, up 0.8 percentage points. Both measures remain green, with procurement below the <=30-day target and payments above the >=95% target. The recovery in payment timeliness indicates the year-end receiving certification and Grants/Budget huddles addressed the prior quarter’s friction. Procurement also benefited from the new standard scope library for facilities maintenance, small equipment, and professional services amendments.
periods.recommendations: Continue the receiving certification process at quarter-end, not just year-end, for departments with high purchase-order volume. Expand the standard scope library to include recurring coastal maintenance, records digitization, and traffic signal support contracts. To preserve control discipline, Internal Audit should perform a light-touch sample of expedited 2026-Q1 procurements and confirm that documentation remained complete.

periods.analysis: Harborview stayed in a strong green position in 2026-Q2: Procurement Cycle Time increased slightly from 24 days to 25 days, up 1 day quarter-over-quarter, while remaining well within the <=30-day target. Invoices Paid Within 30 Days improved from 96.6% to 97.1%, up 0.5 percentage points and above the >=95% target. The small procurement increase is consistent with early summer activity, including lifeguard equipment, road-striping materials, and the North Harbor permitting counter remodel. The payment improvement shows that the quarter-end receiving controls are becoming routine rather than exceptional.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the current procurement lane model, standard scope library, and quarter-end receiving certification through the 2026-Q3 summer volume period. Add a 25-day early-warning flag in Munis so buyers intervene before any requisition threatens the 30-day ceiling. Extend the AP exception process to include vendor master-data issues, particularly expired W-9s and ACH changes, to protect the 97.1% payment performance.

periods.analysis: Available procurement cycle time is 34 days against a 30-day ceiling, while invoices paid within 30 days are 97.1% against a 95% target. These carried-forward figures show a mixed result, not a uniformly healthy purchasing process; the procurement value also needs source verification.
periods.recommendations: Check the procurement spreadsheet and aged files, assign owners to verified delays, and preserve the AP aging controls that support timely payment.
